The United States Marine Corps. The United States Marine Corps is an amphibious and expeditionary military branch established in seventeen seventy-five that evolved from a small maritime guard into a global power-projection force. During World War II, the Marines became the icon of American offensive power in the Pacific, executing island-hopping campaigns against Japan and defining the doctrine and mythology of modern amphibious warfare.

Officially established in seventeen seventy-five alongside the Continental Navy, the Marines initially served as shipboard security and boarding parties. By the twentieth century, they had evolved into a distinct expeditionary force specialized in rapid-deployment operations. The Marine Corps philosophy emphasized aggressive small-unit tactics, leadership at all levels, and rapid decision-making. This culture made them effective in the chaotic, decentralized fighting of island warfare against Japanese forces.

In World War II, the Marines executed the island-hopping strategy across the Pacific: Guadalcanal between nineteen forty-two and forty-three, Iwo Jima in nineteen forty-five, and Okinawa in nineteen forty-five. These were brutal assaults against entrenched Japanese defenders that inflicted staggering casualties on both sides. Iwo Jima in February and March of nineteen forty-five became the iconic Marine engagement. Seventy thousand Marines fought twenty-two thousand Japanese defenders in brutal mountain and cave warfare. The iconic flag-raising photograph became the symbol of American sacrifice and victory.

Marine casualties in the Pacific were extraordinary: tens of thousands killed and wounded. Their aggressive tactics and willingness to accept heavy losses became both celebrated as courage and commitment, and controversial as potential waste. After nineteen forty-five, the Marines developed amphibious assault doctrine, helicopter-borne operations, and specialized training. Their institutional culture emphasizing unit cohesion, leadership, and aggressive offense became central to their identity and public mythology.
